chip-capabilities.title: What the NTC thermistor (generic) does
chip-capabilities.alt: Capability map of the NTC thermistor (generic): Voltage divider (supported): Turns the voltage at the divider node into the thermistor's resistance, thermistor low side or high side; Beta equation (supported): Temperature from R25 and B (B25/85 by default), in fixed point, inside the rated window you declare; Steinhart-Hart (supported): Temperature from the three Steinhart-Hart coefficients, in integers; Resistance table (supported): Temperature from a table of resistance and temperature rows, interpolated in ln R; any part is data; Open, short and range faults (supported): Names a cut wire, a short, a part outside its window, noisy samples and an ADC that disagrees; Reading uncertainty (supported): Bounds every reading from the tolerances you declare and one converter step; Self-heating (supported): Estimates the power the divider dissipates in the thermistor, to size the series resistor; Switched bias (supported): Switches the divider supply from an MCU pin and waits for it to settle, to cut current and self-heating.
chip-capabilities.description: Each card is one function of the NTC thermistor (generic): an icon, its name and what it does for the application. The filled pill says how this driver covers it (legend below); the outlined pills are the chip registers behind it. The coverage table in the README gives the driver calls and the datasheet section of each card.

chip-hero.title: NTC thermistor (generic)
chip-hero.alt: Overview of the NTC thermistor (generic), a resistor whose resistance falls as it heats: with a series resistor it makes a voltage divider an ADC can read, and a curve (a table, Steinhart-Hart coefficients, or R25 and B) turns the resistance into a temperature. A MCU talks to it over ADC input; it reads back Temperature. Headline figures: 10 kΩ resistance at 25 °C, ±1 % (the example part); 3435 K B value at 25/85 °C, ±1 % (the example part); -40 to 150 °C operating temperature (the example part); 0.31 mA permissive operating current at 25 °C (the example part).
chip-hero.description: The NTC thermistor (generic) in the middle, drawn as its 0603 package. On the left the MCU that runs the driver, joined to it by ADC input. Below it, what the chip reads back. The tiles at the bottom are the headline numbers, each with the datasheet section and page it comes from.

conversion-pipeline.title: From an ADC code to a temperature
conversion-pipeline.alt: Pipeline of six stages: the mean of the samples, the classification of the code as open circuit, short circuit or out of scale, the divider's node ratio giving the resistance, the curve (table, Steinhart-Hart or beta) giving the temperature, the window and offset, and the uncertainty bound.
conversion-pipeline.description: Top to bottom, each arrow hands one number to the next stage. Read() takes sample_count codes and their mean (the spread check can stop it as Unstable). The mean code is classified: at or above 2^bits is CodeOutOfScale, a code in the margin at the open rail is OpenCircuit, one in the margin at the short rail is ShortCircuit; which rail is which depends on the divider side. The node ratio gives the thermistor's resistance from the series resistor, in 1/256 ohm. The resistance goes through the curve: a table (a bounded binary search, then linear interpolation in ln R) or Steinhart-Hart (a cubic in ln R) or the beta equation (1/T in Q32), any of them with no floating point and no library. The temperature must lie inside the window; the offset is added last. The uncertainty bound is computed from the same code. The stages are the functions of inc/ntc_thermistor_conversion.hpp.

driver-layers.title: The layers, one of them yours
driver-layers.alt: Layer diagram: your application calls the NtcThermistor core, which asks for ADC conversions through the ADC port contract to the port class you write, which reads the divider; the core and the contract are the same on every MCU.
driver-layers.description: Top to bottom, each arrow is a call. Your application calls one object, whose public calls are listed from the umbrella header in inc/. The core turns each call into register reads and writes and hands them to the port contract (the CRTP base in inc/*_interface.hpp), which forwards them, at compile time, to the hooks of the port class you write; your port moves the bytes on the bus. The notes on the right say which layers stay the same on every MCU and which one you write. A library without a port contract has only the first two layers.
